title: Ignition of a hot hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen mixture at constant pressure

outcome.label: Completed, with differences from what was expected

goal: The first case with burning. Chemistry alone, with no flow. Step 3 of 7 on the way to a rotating detonation engine.
story: Solved with OpenFOAM's chemistry solver by a fresh agent, which also wrote an independent solution of its own to check both OpenFOAM and the reference. gpucfd had no chemistry. A chemistry kernel for the GPU was built the same day and run on the same parcel. It is not yet joined to gpucfd's flow solver.

requirements: A parcel of hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen at rest, suddenly at \(1000\,\mathrm{K}\). The pressure is held at 2 atmospheres and no heat is exchanged.
After a short delay the mixture ignites and burns. Nothing flows, so only time matters.
The full hydrogen reaction scheme: 10 species and 27 reactions.
Asked for: temperature against time, the ignition time, the final temperature, the species, whether atoms and energy are kept, and what the chemistry costs.
Reference: an independent chemistry program (CHEMKIN II) with the same reaction scheme.
Required: ignition time within 1 %, final temperature within 0.1 %, the atoms of each element constant within 0.001 %.

results.headline: Completed, with one difference from what was expected. OpenFOAM ignites the mixture at \(217.709\,\mathrm{\mu s}\), \(0.028\,\%\) before the reference (required: within \(1\,\%\)), and ends at \(2220.54\,\mathrm{K}\), \(0.0016\,\%\) above it (required: \(0.1\,\%\)). gpucfd's new chemistry kernel solves the same parcel: ignition at 217.72 microseconds (-0.022 % from the reference) and \(2220.45\,\mathrm{K}\) at the end. For one parcel the GPU is slower than OpenFOAM on one core (15 s against 11 s for 80000 steps); its gain is in numbers: 4096 parcels take 6 s, and a million cells before ignition advance at about 199 million cells x steps per second (OpenFOAM's chemistry on a mesh of many cells was not timed, so there is no fair ratio yet).
meaning: All three requirements are met with a wide margin. OpenFOAM agrees with the agent's independent solution about forty times more closely than either agrees with the reference, so what is left is mostly the reference's own accuracy.
One prediction of the agent was wrong: it expected OpenFOAM's shipped example to miss the 1 %. It is inside, at 0.56 %.

For the detonation engine: in OpenFOAM the time step is an accuracy setting of the chemistry, not only of the flow. Halving the step halves the error, and no setting of the chemistry solver removes it.

For the detonation engine: the chemistry of one cell costs about 100 microseconds per time step on one core, and far more while the cell ignites. The flow part cost 0.3 microseconds per cell in step 1. This is why chemistry on the GPU matters.

gpucfd's new chemistry kernel meets the same three requirements. With the same constants it agrees with OpenFOAM to one part in ten million. With a million cells it advances about 200 million cells times steps per second, at the time step a flow solver with shock waves takes.
limits: gpucfd is worse for few cells: slower than OpenFOAM for one cell, and no gain below about 10 000 cells.
There is no fair ratio of the two tools' chemistry cost yet. OpenFOAM's chemistry was timed on one cell only; gpucfd's speed is for a million cells at a looser tolerance and in mixed precision.
gpucfd's kernel is chemistry alone, tested with this one reaction scheme. It is not yet joined to the flow solver.
One cell only. The cost per cell in a real flow depends on how many cells are igniting at the same time.
The reference states no accuracy of its own. The agent's independent solution suggests it is good to about 0.03 %.
answer: Both tools meet all three requirements, with a wide margin: the ignition time is right to a few hundredths of a per cent.
One prediction of the agent was wrong: OpenFOAM's shipped example is more accurate than it expected.
For one cell the GPU is slower than OpenFOAM. Its gain comes with many cells, which is what a detonation needs.

accuracy.note: Each number is how far the computed value is from the reference, an independent chemistry program, with the smallest time step. Zero would be a perfect match. The first three rows are the problem's requirements.

head: Run
OpenFOAM
gpucfd
rows: 4096 parcels at once, 80000 time steps (gpucfd's default setting)
speed.note: One cell, with the same very tight tolerance in both tools. Looser settings and a simpler chemistry solver gave OpenFOAM the same answer in under a third of the time. One cell is the wrong job for a GPU: one of its thousands of threads works alone. The last row is what it is for. gpucfd's times run from creating the solver to the final field; starting the GPU library adds 0.26 s once.
